segments.text:
- The test runs on the development machine (x86-64 CPUs).
- That machine has no compiler for AArch64, the instruction set of CRB. So the test never assembles the asm text of the kernels.
- **Round 5** is the set of additions that makes `bwx12.c` from `bwx11.c`. It is not a round of a measurement.
- **New kernels** means the 26 kernels that round 5 added. It does not mean the new read kernel of the whole-chip test.
segments.heading: File header: what the test is and how to run it

segments.text:
Step 1, the source text.
- `bwx12.c` marks each addition: a comment line `bwx12+` stands before it and a comment line `bwx12-` after it.
- Without these blocks the file must be `bwx11.c`, byte for byte. The test compares the sha256 with the value in `ref-bwx11/build.txt`, the record of the accepted bwx11 build.
- The same rule holds for the self-test source.

Step 2, a local build.
- On x86-64, `bwx12.c` compiles each asm or NEON kernel as a plain C loop, a **stand-in**.
- The test builds two programs with the same script `build12.sh`: one from `bwx12.c`, one from the bwx11 text.
- `--list` prints the kernel names. 29 kernels of bwx11 plus 26 new kernels gives 55 names.
- The checker `check_listing12.py` must find the same machine code and the same loop offset for the 29 kernels in both builds. `--skip-new` leaves out its rules for the 26 new kernels.
- **Loop offset**: the address of the loop start modulo 64.

Step 3, the AArch64 text.
- `gcc -E` runs only the preprocessor: it expands macros and includes. With `-D__aarch64__` it prints the AArch64 branch of the source. Nothing is compiled.
- The test takes the asm text of each new kernel from that output and writes it in the format of an `objdump` listing.
- The compiler adds a frame around some kernels: stores of d8 to d15 before the loop and loads after it. The test cannot see the real frame. It writes the frame of the accepted bwx11 listing. The comment calls this an assumption.
- The function start is the next 64 B boundary plus the pad of the `PLACE` macro.
- This listing, put after the accepted bwx11 listing, must pass the checker.

Step 4, changed copies.
- The test changes one kernel of that listing and runs the checker again. The checker must fail.
- The comment names four kinds of change. The code runs seven cases (line 268). One of them is of a fifth kind: a missing `movi`.

- Start the script with no argument, for example `python3 test_kernels12.py`.
- With the environment variable `KEEP=1` the temporary folder is kept. It holds the two builds and the listings.
- Output: one line `PASS name` or `FAIL name: detail` per check.
- Exit status 0 means that every check passed.
Modules of the Python standard library. `hashlib` computes sha256. `subprocess` starts other programs. `tempfile` creates the temporary folder.

- `HERE`: the folder of this script. The paths of all source and reference files start from it, so the script can be started from any folder.
- `REF`: the folder `ref-bwx11` beside the script. It holds the build record, the listing and the offsets table of the accepted bwx11 build.
- Lines 42-43 load `check_listing12.py` of the same folder as the module `cl`. The test takes two things from it: the names of the 26 new kernels (the keys of its table `NEW`) and its two end-pointer instructions. The test does not read the expected loops of `NEW`. Only the checker process compares with them.
- `fails` counts the failed checks.

Prints `PASS name` or `FAIL name: detail` for one check.
- `ok` is the result of the check.
- The detail is printed only when the check failed and a detail was given.
- Line 51 adds 1 to `fails` for a failed check. A failed check does not stop the script.
segments.heading: Function `check`: print one result line

segments.text:
Returns `text` without its bwx12 blocks.
- A line that is exactly `/* bwx12+ */` starts a block.
- A line that is exactly `/* bwx12- */` ends it.
- The two marker lines and all lines between them are dropped.
- Every other line is kept unchanged, with its line end.
segments.heading: Function `strip12`: remove the bwx12 blocks

segments.text: Starts the command `cmd` and waits until it ends. The returned object holds the exit status (`returncode`), the standard output and the error output as text. Extra arguments such as `env` are passed on.
segments.heading: Function `run`: start a program, keep its output

segments.text: Runs `check_listing12.py` of the same folder as a separate process, with the arguments `args`. `sys.executable` is the Python interpreter that runs this test.
segments.heading: Function `checker`: run check_listing12.py

segments.text: Line 75 reads `ref-bwx11/build.txt` and keeps the lines that start with 64 hexadecimal digits and two spaces. These are the sha256 lines of the accepted bwx11 build [Ref1]. `digests` maps each file name to its sha256.
segments.heading: Function `test_source`: bwx12 source without additions equals bwx11

segments.text:
The loop runs for `bwx12.c` and for `bwx12_selftest.c`.
- Line 77 reads the file and removes the bwx12 blocks.
- Lines 78-79: the check passes when the sha256 of the rest equals the recorded sha256 of `bwx11.c` or `bwx11_selftest.c`. On a failure the detail is the recorded value.
- Line 80 writes the rest into the temporary folder under the bwx11 name. `test_standin` uses it as the reference source.
- A pass proves this: every line outside the marked blocks is the text of the accepted bwx11 source, byte for byte.
Creates the folders `new` and `old` in the temporary folder. `new` gets copies of `bwx12.c`, `bwx12_selftest.c` and `build12.sh`.
segments.heading: Function `test_standin`: local build with and without the new kernels

segments.text:
`old` gets the reference source under the file names of bwx12.
- Lines 90-91: the bwx11 text of `test_source` is saved as `bwx12.c`. Its include line for the self-test is changed to name `bwx12_selftest.c`.
- Line 92: the bwx11 self-test text is saved as `bwx12_selftest.c`.
- Line 93: the same `build12.sh` is copied.
So the same script builds both folders, and both binaries are named `bwx12`.

- Line 94 lists the CPUs that this process may run on, without any CPU above 119.
- `BWX_CPUS`: `build12.sh` restarts itself under `taskset` (a tool that limits a program to a list of CPUs) on this CPU list. Its default list is CPUs 0-119, the CPUs that the tests use on CRB [Ref4]. So the two builds run only on CPUs that the test process may use.
- `BWX_MARKER`: `build12.sh` stops when its marker file exists (by default `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING`). The test names a file that does not exist, so this stop cannot happen here.

- Runs `bash build12.sh` in `new`, then in `old`, with the two variables set.
- Each run compiles `bwx12.c` with gcc, runs the self-test of the binary, and writes `build.txt`, `listing.txt`, `offsets.tsv` and `selftest-bwx12.txt` into its folder [Ref4].
- Both binaries are x86-64 programs with stand-in kernels.
- The check fails when the script ends with a status other than 0. The detail is the last 400 characters of its error output.
- `build12.sh` ends with status 5 when the compile fails, and with status 4 when the self-test fails. It ends with status 6 when its check of the branch targets of the two timed functions of the trial mode fails [Ref4].
- After a failed build the function returns. The checks of lines 101-117 are then not run.

Runs the new binary with `--list`. It prints one kernel name per line and ends [Ref3]. The check passes when there are 55 names and names 30 to 55 equal the keys of `NEW` in `check_listing12.py`, in the same order.

Reads the self-test output of the new build. A result row has the fields kernel, check, bytes, result.
- Line 105 drops the comment lines and the `call,` lines.
- Line 106 counts, for each new kernel, the rows with the result `pass`.
- Line 107 holds the expected counts: 8 for a read kernel, 5 for a write kernel, 8 for a copy kernel [Ref7].
- The text must also contain no `FAIL` and end with `# failures=0`.
Here these rows test the stand-in loops, not the asm kernels.

Runs the checker on the listing of `new`. The listing and the offsets table of `old` are the reference.
- `--ref-binary bwx12`: the blocks of the reference listing have the binary name bwx12 here.
- `--skip-new`: the rules for the 26 new kernels are left out.
- The check passes when the checker ends with status 0 and prints `kernels=29 failed_rows=0`.
- Meaning: each of the 29 kernels of bwx11 has the same instruction text and the same loop offset in both builds [Ref2]. The checker compares `objdump` text. Of the addresses it compares only the loop start modulo 64 and the distance of a branch target from the function start.
- This result holds for the x86-64 build only.

`build12.sh` writes one line that starts with `## placement bwx12` into `build.txt`. It lists the start address modulo 64 of `call`, `read_smaps`, `tcount`, `timed_sequence` and `timed_sequence_hot`, as far as the binary has these symbols [Ref4].
- `call` runs one kernel on a part of a buffer. In the interval mode (option `--seq`) the thread function `worker` reads the clock and calls it [Ref3]. The whole-chip test uses this mode [Ref9].
- `timed_sequence` and `timed_sequence_hot` are the timed functions of the trial mode. The whole-chip test does not use that mode.
The check passes when both builds have this line and the two lines are equal.

- `FRAME`: the instructions that the test writes before the loop of a kernel whose clobber list names v8. `stp` stores two registers. The four `stp` store d8 to d15 to the stack.
- `END` is a placeholder. Line 188 puts the end-pointer instruction there.
- `UNFRAME`: the four `ldp` that load d8 to d15 back after the loop.
- This is the frame of `asmread` and `asmcopy` in the accepted bwx11 listing [Ref8]. For the new kernels it is an assumption of the test.
segments.heading: Assumed frame of a kernel that uses v8 to v15

segments.text:
- Lines 126-128 create a folder `stub` with an empty file `arm_neon.h`. The AArch64 branch of `bwx12.c` includes this header, and the x86-64 gcc does not have it.
- Line 129 runs `gcc -E -P -D__aarch64__` on `bwx12.c`. `-E`: expand macros and includes only, do not compile, assemble or link. `-P`: leave out the marker lines that give file name and line number. `-D__aarch64__`: select the AArch64 branch of the source. `-I`: search the folder `stub` for headers.
- Lines 130-131 stop with an error when gcc fails. The message is the last 400 characters of the gcc messages.
segments.heading: Function `aarch64_functions`: asm text of each new kernel

segments.text:
For each of the 26 new kernels, the pattern of line 135 finds two things that stand one after the other in the gcc output:
- the `PLACE` statement of the kernel: an `__asm__(...)` that holds only string literals,
- the function `k_<name>` with its parameter list and its body.
Lines 137-138 stop with an error when a kernel is not found. Line 139 joins the strings of the `PLACE` statement. Line 140 takes the expression after `.fill` and computes its value. This value `pad` is the number of zero bytes between the 64 B boundary and the function start [Ref3].

A gcc asm statement has the form `__asm__ volatile(template : outputs : inputs : clobbers)`. The template is a row of string literals.
- Lines 142-156 start at the first `__asm__ volatile(` of the body. They collect each string literal up to the first colon outside a string. This is the template.
- Line 157 keeps the text from that colon to the next `);` as `operands`: the operand lists and the clobber list.
- Line 158 joins the literals and turns the escape sequences for line end and tab into real characters. The result `asm` is the assembler text of the kernel.
- The captured body can be longer than the function. gcc prints a kernel that a macro defines on one line, and the pattern ends the body at a line that starts with `}`. So only the first asm statement is used.

- Line 159: a kernel is a copy kernel when its parameter list holds the words `restrict d`.
- Line 160 names the register for each operand of the template. Read and write kernels: pointer `p` in x0, `end` in x1, value `v` in x2. Copy kernels: destination `d` in x0, source `s` in x1, `end` in x2.
- The test sets these registers. They are the registers of the same operands in the accepted bwx11 listing [Ref8].

Turns the assembler text into a flat list of instructions.
- Line 163 removes the white space at both ends of a line and replaces each operand `%[name]` by its register.
- `.rept N` and `.endr` are assembler directives: the lines between them are repeated N times. Lines 166-173 do this repeat here. For `read_nop256` the result holds 256 `nop` lines.
- Empty lines are skipped.

- `1:` is the label at the loop start. The lines before it run once per call (`init`). The lines after it are the loop.
- The last line must be `b.lo 1b`: branch back to label 1 while the pointer is below the end. If it is not, lines 178-179 stop with an error.
- Line 180 removes this line. `synth` writes the branch later, with its address.

`spell` writes a number as `objdump` prints it. The decimal number after `#` becomes hexadecimal in two instruction forms: `add` of x registers and `movi`. Example: `add x0, x0, #256` becomes `add x0, x0, #0x100`. Line 185 applies it to `init` and to the loop.

- Line 186: the end-pointer instruction, as `check_listing12.py` expects it. For a read or write kernel it is `add x1, x0, x1, lsl #3`: end = start + 8 B per 64-bit word.
- The asm text does not hold the end-pointer instruction. On CRB the compiler makes it from a C statement of the kernel function. The test writes it here. Line 189 also adds the `ret` after the loop.
- Line 187: `framed` is true when the clobber list names `v8`.
- Line 188: a framed kernel gets the lines of `FRAME`, with the end-pointer instruction at the place of `END`. Any other kernel gets the end-pointer instruction only.
- Line 189 stores per kernel: pad, instructions before the loop, loop, instructions after the loop, operand text.

Writes the 26 kernels one after the other. The first address is `start`, 0x6000 by default (a multiple of 64).
- Lines 198-199: an optional function `change` may alter the pad or the instruction lists of a kernel. Step 4 uses it.
- Line 200: the function start is the next multiple of 64 B, plus `pad`. This is the rule of the `PLACE` macro [Ref3].
- Line 201: the loop starts after the instructions of `head`. Each AArch64 instruction is 4 B long.
segments.heading: Function `synth`: write listing text and offsets rows

segments.text:
- Line 202 writes the block title and the function line in the format of `listing.txt`.
- Lines 203-206 write one line per instruction, with its address. After the loop instructions they write the loop branch as `objdump` prints it: `b.cc` to the loop start. `b.cc` and `b.lo` are the same instruction.
- Line 208 writes the row of the offsets table: binary, kernel, function, start, loop start, loop start modulo 64.
- The function returns the listing text and the offsets rows.

- Lines 213-218: get the 26 kernels from `aarch64_functions`. When it stops with one of its three errors (lines 131, 138, 179), one check fails and the function returns. If not, the check passes when 26 kernels were found.
- Lines 219-220 read the listing and the offsets table of the accepted bwx11 build. They change the binary name in them from bwx11 to bwx12. The checker then reads them as the first 29 kernels of a bwx12 build.
segments.heading: Function `test_aarch64_text`: the asm text against the checker

segments.text:
`result` builds one checker input and runs the checker.
- The listing file is the accepted bwx11 listing plus the 26 blocks of `synth`. The offsets file is built the same way.
- The checker is called without options. Its reference is then the same accepted bwx11 build.
- So the 29 old kernels are compared with a copy of themselves and cannot differ. Only the rules for the 26 new kernels can fail.

Step 3. The unchanged listing must pass: exit status 0, 29 old rows and 26 new rows without a failure. The checker rules for a new kernel are [Ref2]:
- The loop holds exactly the expected instructions with every operand. For `read_nop256`: 8 `ldp`, 256 `nop`, `add`, `cmp`. The loop ends with the branch `b.cc` to the loop start.
- Before the loop stand only the end pointer, stores of d registers and the expected `movi` or `dup`. After the loop stand only loads of d registers, and the last instruction is `ret`.
- The loop offset is 20 B for a read kernel, 40 B for a write kernel, 52 B for a copy kernel. It equals the loop offset of `asmread`, `asmwrite` or `asmcopy` in the same listing. The row of the offsets table gives the same value.
- The function has one backward branch and no other branch. Each of d8 to d15 that the loop uses is stored before the loop and loaded after it.
A pass shows that the asm text and the pads of `bwx12.c` agree with the checker, if the frame is as assumed.

Checks the clobber list of each new kernel.
- `used`: the numbers of all q and v registers in the instructions before the loop and in the loop.
- `named`: the numbers of the v registers in the clobber list.
- The check fails when a used register is not named.
gcc does not read the asm text. The vector registers of the text are not operands. So gcc learns only from the clobber list that the text changes them.
`one_nop_less(victim)` returns a change function for `synth`. It removes one `nop` from the loop of the kernel `victim`. All other kernels stay unchanged.
segments.heading: Step 4: changed copies that the checker must reject

segments.text: In `read_dadd8`, one add gets the source register v24 in place of v2. The loop loads v2. It does not load v24. The number of instructions stays the same.
Adds 4 B to the pad of `write_nop96`. The function and its loop start move by 4 B, the length of one instruction. The loop offset becomes 44 B in place of 40 B.

In `read_iadd16`, the first frame instruction is replaced by `sub sp, sp, #0x40`. The original instruction stores d8 and d9 and moves the stack pointer down by 64 B. The replacement only moves the stack pointer. So d8 and d9 are never stored.

In `read_dadd2`, the instruction `movi v16.4s, #0x0` is removed.
- It sets v16 to 0 before the loop. The first add of the loop collects its sum in v16.
- The pad grows by 4 B, so the loop start keeps its address. The loop offset rule can therefore not report this change.

Runs the checker on 7 changed listings, one change per run.
- `failed`: the kernel names of the checker output rows that contain `FAIL`.
- A check passes only when the checker ends with status 1 and `failed` holds exactly the changed kernel.
- So each check proves two things. The checker fails the row of the changed kernel. It fails no other row. The test does not compare the reason that the checker prints.
- The first case is `read_nop256` with 255 `nop`. The whole-chip test runs this kernel in part L.

- Line 281 creates a new temporary folder. Its name starts with `bwx12-test-`.
- Lines 283-285 run the three test functions in this order. `test_standin` needs the files that `test_source` wrote.
- Lines 286-290 run even when a test function stops with an error. When the environment variable `KEEP` is set and not empty, the folder is kept and its path is printed. If not, the folder is deleted.
- Lines 291-292 print the number of failed checks. The return value is 1 if a check failed and 0 if not. After an error that no test function handles, these two lines are not run. Python then prints a traceback and ends with status 1.
segments.heading: Function `main`: run the three test functions

segments.text: When the file is started as a script, the return value of `main` becomes the exit status of the process.
